The rain had stopped an hour ago, but water still dripped through the cracked skylight in slow, deliberate taps.

No one spoke.

Mara lay on an old checkout counter beneath the faded sign for canned peaches. Her jacket had been rolled up under her head. Someone—Eli, probably—had covered her with a blanket that still smelled faintly of smoke.

Her left hand was clenched around the edge of the counter.

Her right arm was wrapped in a strip of shirt torn from Tomas’s sleeve.

The blood had soaked through anyway.

“We don’t know,” Tomas said for the third time.

His voice was too loud in the empty grocery store. It bounced off bare shelves and broken freezer doors.

“We don’t know it always happens.”

Eli looked at him from beside Mara’s feet. He was nineteen, maybe twenty, but the past year had narrowed him into something older. There was dried mud on his face and a cut across his lip.

“We do know,” he said.

Tomas shook his head. “No. We’ve seen people get sick. That doesn’t mean—”

“Her fever’s already started.”

As if summoned by the words, Mara shuddered under the blanket.

Nia knelt beside her, pressing a damp cloth to Mara’s forehead. Her hands were steady. That was the worst of it. Nia’s hands were always steady when everyone else’s had begun to shake.

Mara opened her eyes.

For a moment, there was only confusion there. Then she saw them gathered around her: Tomas standing by the aisle of rotten cereal, Eli near the counter, Nia beside her.

And she knew.

“No,” Tomas said immediately, as if she had said something aloud.

Mara’s mouth twitched. “I didn’t ask.”

“You were going to.”

“I was thinking it.”

“That’s the same thing.”

A thin, broken laugh escaped her, but it turned into a cough. Nia helped her sit up. The blanket slipped from Mara’s shoulder, exposing the bandage around her arm.

The bite was hidden beneath it.

No one looked directly at it anymore.

Outside, something moaned in the street. Long and hollow. Another voice answered from farther away.

Mara listened until the sound faded.

“We can move,” Tomas said. He was speaking quickly now, building a plan out of panic. “There’s a clinic two blocks east. Maybe there are antibiotics. Maybe there’s something in the records. People used to say—”

“People used to say a lot of things,” Nia said softly.

Tomas rounded on her. “So that’s it? We just—what? Put a bullet in her because it’s easier?”

The word hung in the air.

Mara closed her eyes.

Eli stared at the floor.

Nia’s expression did not change, but her fingers tightened around the damp cloth. “It is not easier.”

Tomas’s face crumpled then. Not all at once. First his jaw went slack. Then his shoulders folded inward. He put both hands over his mouth, and the sound he made behind them was small and animal.

Mara reached for him with her good hand.

“Tomas.”

He didn’t move.

“Tomas,” she said again.

He stepped forward at last and took her hand. He dropped to his knees beside the counter, pressing his forehead against her knuckles.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

“For what?”

“I should’ve seen it. I should’ve been closer. I had the crowbar, I had—”

“You had three of them on you.”

“I should’ve gotten there.”

“You did get there.”

“Not soon enough.”

Mara looked past him toward the dark front windows. Rainwater streaked the glass. Beyond it, the world was gray and emptied out: overturned cars, weeds splitting the pavement, a child’s red bicycle lying on its side in the middle of the road.

“We don’t get soon enough anymore,” she said.

Tomas began to cry harder.

Eli turned away. His hand rested on the pistol at his belt.

Nia saw it.

“No,” she said.

Eli looked at her. “It has to be someone.”

“It doesn’t have to be you.”

“It should be.”

“Why?”

He swallowed. “Because she saved me.”

Mara opened her eyes again. “That’s exactly why it shouldn’t be you.”

He gave a humorless smile. “You always have an answer.”

“Only because I’ve had more time to practice being scared than you have.”

The fever was taking hold. They could see it now in the shine of her skin, the tremor beneath her words. Her pupils were too wide. Her breathing came in shallow, uneven pulls.

Nia checked her watch.

No one asked why.

“We need to decide,” Nia said.

Tomas stood abruptly. “No.”

“Nine minutes, maybe less.”

“No.”

“If she turns in here—”

“No!”

The shout made everyone flinch.

Outside, the distant moaning stopped.

The silence that followed was worse.

Tomas looked at Mara. Really looked at her. At the woman who had taught him to set snares and read old road maps. The woman who had split her last canteen with him during the drought. The woman who had slapped him awake when he wanted to lie down in the snow and never stand again.

His anger drained out of him.

“What do you want?” he asked.

Mara’s lips parted. She took a long time to answer.

“I don’t want to hurt anyone.”

Nia bowed her head.

“I don’t want to wake up inside myself and not be me,” Mara continued. “I don’t want you to have to run from my face.”

Tomas shook his head, tears falling freely now.

“I’m still here,” she said. “Please. Let me stay that way.”

Eli drew the pistol.

The sound of it clearing the holster seemed impossibly final.

Tomas made a choking sound and grabbed Mara’s hand tighter.

“I can’t,” Eli said.

Mara looked at Nia.

Nia did not take the gun immediately. Her gaze moved over each of them, as if committing them to memory: Eli’s terrified stillness, Tomas folded over Mara’s hand, Mara’s pale face beneath the flickering emergency light.

Then she reached out.

Eli placed the pistol in her palm.

Mara exhaled.

“Wait,” Tomas said.

Everyone froze.

He leaned over Mara and kissed her forehead. He stayed there for a long moment, eyes shut, his face pressed against her skin.

When he pulled back, he was shaking so violently he could barely stand.

“I love you,” he said.

Mara smiled, faintly. “I know.”

Then she looked at Eli.

“Keep your knife sharp,” she told him.

His face broke. He nodded once.

Finally, she looked at Nia.

“Do it before I’m gone.”

Nia raised the pistol.

Mara’s eyes stayed on her.

There was no speech. No prayer. No final comfort large enough to fill the space between one heartbeat and the next.

Nia’s hand trembled for the first time.

“I’m sorry,” she whispered.

Mara’s expression softened.

“I’m not.”

The shot was deafening.

For several seconds, no one moved.

Then the sound rolled away into the hollow store, through the broken aisles and empty shelves, out into the wet streets where the dead would hear it.

Tomas remained kneeling beside the counter, still holding Mara’s hand.

It was warm for a little while longer.

At first, it was only a shape in the corner of the room.

Not a face. Not even a body. Just a suggestion of someone standing where no one should have been—beside the pantry door, at the end of the hallway, reflected briefly in the dark window above the sink. Each time, he turned too quickly and found nothing but furniture, coats, the harmless geometry of his own home.

He told himself it was exhaustion.

The murder had left him exhausted in ways sleep could not touch. He had imagined guilt as a sharp thing, a blade lodged beneath the ribs. Instead it was damp. It crept through him slowly, spoiling everything it reached. Food tasted faintly of pennies. Water sat thick and warm in his throat. His hands, no matter how long he scrubbed them, seemed to retain a smell he could not name: rust, earth, something sweet beginning to turn.

He replayed the moment constantly, though never in full. His mind protected him at first. It gave him flashes: the victim’s widened eyes; the sound of breath stopping; the impossible heaviness of a body once it had become only a body. He would be washing a cup or waiting for a light to change, and the memory would slide into him like cold water down the spine.

Then the shape began to resemble the victim.

Only in fragments. A sleeve disappearing around a doorway. A familiar tilt of the head glimpsed in the television’s black screen. Once, he saw their hand resting on the arm of his chair: pale, still, fingers bent in the same awkward position they had been when he left them.

He blinked, and the hand was gone.

That was when he stopped sleeping with the lights off.

Darkness no longer felt empty. It felt occupied. Every unlit room held its breath. He began leaving lamps burning through the night, filling the house with a jaundiced glow that made the corners look deeper, not safer. The electric bill came, then another. He let the envelopes pile up unopened. There were more urgent things to fear.

The ghost never spoke. That was the worst part.

If it had accused him, he thought he could have argued. He had rehearsed excuses in the shower, in traffic, while staring at his own reflection: It was an accident. You made me do it. I didn’t mean to. But the figure in the corner only watched. Its silence became a kind of judgment too vast for words.

Soon he began speaking first.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered to the hallway.

No answer.

“I didn’t have a choice.”

The floorboards creaked somewhere beyond the bedroom door.

He started arranging objects carefully. Knives had to face inward in the drawer. Shoes had to be aligned beside the bed. He checked the locks seven times before sleep and seven times after waking, though he could no longer remember what he thought was trying to get in. Sometimes he found the front door unlocked in the morning and stood staring at it for hours, certain the victim had entered during the night.

Or perhaps, worse, that they had never left.

His world shrank to the size of the house. Outside, people’s laughter sounded obscene. Cashiers looked at him too long. Strangers on the street seemed to pause when he passed, their eyes flicking toward his hands. He became convinced the crime was visible on him, not in any obvious way, but in small betrayals: the way he held his shoulders, the way he flinched at sirens, the shadow beneath his fingernails that no soap could erase.

He stopped answering calls. He stopped opening curtains.

The ghost appeared more often.

It stood at the foot of his bed one night, clearer than before. The victim looked neither angry nor wounded. Their face was simply empty, stripped of everything that had made it familiar. Their eyes seemed fixed on him with the patient attention of someone waiting for a confession.

He screamed.

When the lights came on, he was alone. But the mattress beside him had sunk slightly, as though someone had just risen from it.

After that, he no longer trusted his senses. He found whispers in the hum of the refrigerator, accusations in the pipes, footsteps in rain against the windows. He began to wonder whether the ghost was truly there or whether it had grown from some rotten place inside him. The question gave him no comfort. If it was real, he was haunted. If it was not, then he had become the haunted place.

The murder had begun as a single act, contained in a single terrible night.

But it did not stay there.

It spread into his mornings, his rooms, his body. It hollowed him out and filled the hollow with dread. Every memory became contaminated by it. Every silence belonged to the victim. Even his own reflection began to seem unfamiliar: a pale man with sleepless eyes, watching from behind the glass, looking increasingly like someone who knew what he had done.

And always, just beyond the edge of his vision, someone stood waiting.

Darkness no longer felt empty. It felt occupied. Every unlit room held its breath. He began leaving lamps burning through the night, filling the house with a jaundiced glow that made the corners look deeper, not safer. The electric bill came, then another. He let the envelopes pile up unopened. There were more urgent things to fear.

The ghost never spoke. That was the worst part.

If it had accused him, he thought he could have argued. He had rehearsed excuses in the shower, in traffic, while staring at his own reflection: It was an accident. You made me do it. I didn’t mean to. But the figure in the corner only watched. Its silence became a kind of judgment too vast for words.

Soon he began speaking first.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered to the hallway.

No answer.

“I didn’t have a choice.”

The floorboards creaked somewhere beyond the bedroom door.

He started arranging objects carefully. Knives had to face inward in the drawer. Shoes had to be aligned beside the bed. He checked the locks seven times before sleep and seven times after waking, though he could no longer remember what he thought was trying to get in. Sometimes he found the front door unlocked in the morning and stood staring at it for hours, certain the victim had entered during the night.

His world shrank to the size of the house. Outside, people’s laughter sounded obscene. Cashiers looked at him too long. Strangers on the street seemed to pause when he passed, their eyes flicking toward his hands. He became convinced the crime was visible on him, not in any obvious way, but in small betrayals: the way he held his shoulders, the way he flinched at sirens, the shadow beneath his fingernails that no soap could erase.

He stopped answering calls. He stopped opening curtains.

It stood at the foot of his bed one night, clearer than before. The victim looked neither angry nor wounded. Their face was simply empty, stripped of everything that had made it familiar. Their eyes seemed fixed on him with the patient attention of someone waiting for a confession.

If it was not, then he had become the haunted place.

The murder had begun as a single act, contained in a single terrible night.

It spread into his mornings, his rooms, his body. It hollowed him out and filled the hollow with dread. Every memory became contaminated by it. Every silence belonged to the victim. The wolves drove them through knee-deep snow until the trees thinned and the ground rose into a wall of black stone. There was nowhere left to run.

For one suspended second, the forest went silent except for their ragged breathing.

Then the first wolf lunged.

Its weight struck like a thrown log, knocking them sideways into the drift. Teeth closed around their forearm—not cleanly, not like a cut, but with a crushing, grinding pressure that seemed to travel straight into the bone. The pain arrived a heartbeat later: white-hot, shocking, so bright it erased thought.

And then came the blood.

It spilled beneath the torn sleeve in sudden warmth, almost startling against the snow. The air had been gnawing at their face, turning fingers and cheeks numb, but the blood was unbearably hot—thick and slick against their skin, steaming faintly where it touched the blue-white ground. For an instant, the contrast was worse than the bite itself: fire pouring from their arm while the cold swallowed everything around it.

The snow beneath them darkened.

The wolf released, growling, and the warmth began to fade almost at once. Cold crept into the wound, sharp and merciless, while the pack closed in.

Rain fell in silver sheets over New Carthage, turning the neon alleys into rivers of fractured color.

Mara Venn followed the bounty beacon through the abandoned transit district, her boots splashing softly over cracked solar tiles. Above her, the old maglev tracks hung between towers like the ribs of some colossal dead animal.

Her target, Kellan Rusk, was somewhere ahead.

The warrant painted his face across the inside of Mara’s visor: former security engineer, wanted for sabotage, theft of restricted navigation codes, and the deaths of three corporate pilots when a freight shuttle fell out of the sky.

Alive preferred.

“Rusk,” Mara called into the dark station concourse. “Your exit routes are sealed.”

A laugh echoed from behind a row of rusted ticket gates.

“You hunters always say that.”

Then the gates exploded outward.

Rusk came through the debris fast, armored in scavenged riot gear and carrying a compact pulse pistol. Mara dropped behind a concrete pillar as blue-white bolts snapped past, leaving smoking holes in the wall.

He ran for the far platform.

Mara pursued.

Her suit fed her distances, angles, probable trajectories. Rusk was quick, but he was injured; his left leg dragged slightly with every third step. He vaulted a fallen maintenance drone, slammed through a service door, and disappeared into the narrow maintenance tunnels beneath the station.

Mara holstered her sidearm and drew a black, baton-shaped device from her belt.

The Arc Lance hummed in her hand.

“Don’t make me use this,” she said, though she knew he could not hear her over the rain and the pounding of his own footsteps.

The tunnel opened into an old power chamber. Emergency lights flickered red across banks of dead machinery. Rusk stood at the far end beside a maintenance lift, one hand on the control panel.

The lift door remained stubbornly shut.

He turned, pulse pistol raised.

Mara froze.

For a moment, neither of them moved.

“You’re not taking me back,” Rusk said.

“Then drop the weapon.”

“You know what they’ll do to me.”

“I know what you did.”

His expression tightened. The pistol came up another fraction.

Mara moved first.

She flicked the Arc Lance forward. Two tethered electrodes shot from its tip with a compressed hiss, trailing hair-thin conductive filaments. One struck Rusk in the chest plate. The other caught the exposed seam beneath his right shoulder.

The weapon discharged.

A sharp crack filled the chamber.

Rusk’s body locked rigidly.

The shock did not throw him backward like the old action feeds promised. Instead, his muscles contracted all at once, violently and without coordination. His fingers clenched around the pistol so tightly that the joints went pale beneath his gloves. His shoulders jerked upward. His jaw snapped shut, trapping a breath behind his teeth.

The pulse disrupted the electrical signals traveling through his nerves—the tiny instructions that normally told his muscles when to flex and relax. For a few terrible seconds, every command became noise.

His arms spasmed. The pistol dropped from his hand and clattered across the floor.

Rusk tried to scream, but the contraction in his chest stole the sound. His breathing became shallow and irregular as the muscles between his ribs seized. His knees buckled, then locked, then buckled again. He fell sideways against the lift controls, slid down the wall, and hit the floor hard.

Mara released the trigger after the weapon’s safety cycle chirped.

The current stopped.

Rusk lay on his back, gasping. His body twitched in smaller aftershocks: fingers curling, one leg jerking against the metal grating. Sweat shone on his forehead despite the cold. His eyes struggled to focus on the ceiling lights.

He tried to push himself up.

Mara was on him before he could rise. She kicked the pulse pistol away, pinned his wrist with a boot, and snapped a restraint band around each arm.

“Stay down,” she said.

Rusk laughed weakly, but it came out as a ragged cough. “That thing… feels worse than dying.”

“It’s designed not to kill you,” Mara replied.

“Comforting.”

She checked his vitals through her visor. Elevated heart rate. Irregular respiration, but stabilizing. No sign of cardiac failure. The Arc Lance had read his body mass and adjusted its output, delivering just enough current to incapacitate without holding the charge long enough to cause lasting injury.

Still, the shock had left him disoriented. His nervous system needed time to reassert its ordinary rhythms. His muscles ached from the forced contractions, and every breath seemed to remind him that his body had briefly ceased to belong to him.

Mara hauled him upright.

Outside, the rain continued to wash the city clean without ever making it clean.

A retrieval skiff descended through the broken roof of the station, its searchlight cutting through the darkness. Rusk squinted up at it, wrists bound, legs unsteady.

“You ever wonder,” he asked, “which side of a bounty makes someone the villain?”

Mara guided him toward the rising platform.

“Every day,” she said.

Then the skiff’s doors opened, and the bounty hunter delivered her target into the future’s cold, waiting hands.

When Mara woke, the first thing she noticed was the sound of water dripping somewhere beyond the walls.

Not rushing water. Not rain. A slow, deliberate drip, each impact clean enough to measure the silence between them.

Then came the smell: rust, antiseptic, old concrete warmed by machinery.

Her eyes opened.

A lamp hung over her face, naked and glaring. She tried to sit up and discovered the restraint around her left wrist: not a shackle exactly, but a broad metal cuff bolted to the arm of the chair. Her other hand was free. Her ankles were strapped down. Across the room, a television screen flickered with gray static.

Mara pulled once against the cuff.

The chair answered with a sharp metallic click.

A pressure band tightened around her forearm.

She froze.

On the table beside her lay a small steel key, just beyond the reach of her fingers. Between the key and her hand sat a compact mechanical device: clean metal, tubes, a clear chamber filled with dark liquid. A message had been taped to its base in block lettering.

**ONE MEASURE OF PAIN.  
ONE MEASURE OF FREEDOM.**

The television crackled to life.

A distorted voice began to speak, calm and almost courteous. It explained the rules without raising its tone. The cuff on her wrist was linked to the chair, the door, and the countdown glowing red on the wall. The key would release her restraints.

But the key would only become reachable when the device registered what it had been built to register: a sacrifice, chosen willingly.

The screen went black.

Mara stared at her reflection in it.

“No,” she said.

The word sounded absurdly small in the room.

She tested the straps at her ankles. Leather, thick and newly fitted. She leaned sideways, trying to tip the chair, but its legs had been welded to a metal plate in the floor. She searched for weak points with her eyes: screws, seams, loose wiring, anything. Her mind moved quickly at first, almost professionally. Inventory. Exit routes. Tools. Leverage.

Then it began circling back to the table.

The device waited in the brightest part of the room.

She refused to look at it directly.

The red digits on the wall changed.

**14:59**

Mara laughed once—a dry, involuntary sound. “You think this makes me who you say I am?”

There was no answer.

She had heard people talk about terror as an overwhelming thing, a flood that swept reason away. This was worse. Terror sharpened her. It made every detail unbearable: the ache in her shoulder from sleeping upright, the cold sweat gathering beneath her collar, the faint pulse visible in her own wrist.

Her free hand trembled.

She closed it into a fist.

The true horror was not the pain promised by the machine. It was the decision. The knowledge that no one was forcing her hand in the immediate, simple sense. The room had been designed so that she would have to become both victim and instrument. Whoever had built it wanted more than blood or suffering. They wanted consent twisted into something ugly.

They wanted her to participate.

“I don’t have to do this,” she whispered.

The timer answered.

**12:41**

Her breathing became too fast. She tried to slow it, counting silently: four in, hold, four out. The old exercise came back from somewhere deep in her memory, something a therapist had taught her after the accident—the accident she had spent years insisting had not been her fault.

Four in.

Hold.

Four out.

Her gaze drifted, against her will, to the steel key.

It gleamed under the lamp.

Mara imagined the door opening. Cold air from the corridor. Her feet on the ground. Her phone, if there was a phone. Police lights. A hospital. Anything beyond this room.

Then she imagined doing what the device demanded.

Her stomach folded in on itself.

She turned her head and retched onto the concrete.

For several seconds, she hung there, coughing, tears leaking from the corners of her eyes. She hated the tears most. They felt like betrayal—her body already surrendering before she had decided anything.

When she finally lifted her head, the timer read **10:06**.

Mara looked at her free hand.

It had always seemed like such an ordinary thing: fingers, knuckles, a crescent scar near the thumb from childhood. She flexed it slowly, feeling each joint obey. The thought of deliberately making that hand suffer filled her with a profound, animal refusal.

Not fear of dying.

Fear of crossing a line inside herself that could never be uncrossed.

She reached for the table, stretching until the cuff pressed painfully into her wrist. Her fingertips brushed cold metal, then slid away. Not close enough.

The device sat there like an accusation.

Mara shut her eyes.

In the darkness behind her lids, she saw every person she had disappointed. Every call she had ignored. Every apology she had postponed because apologizing would mean admitting that the story she told herself—about being practical, being strong, being right—had been a lie.

The trap was cruel. It was monstrous.

But it had found the one truth she could not escape: she wanted to live.

Not nobly. Not bravely. Not in a way that would make sense afterward.

She simply wanted to live.

Her eyes opened.

Her face had gone strangely calm.

With her free hand, she rolled up her sleeve, not because it made the task easier, but because the small act gave her something to control. She wiped her palm against her trousers. Once. Twice. She adjusted her posture against the chair, setting her shoulders as though preparing to lift something heavy.

The timer continued counting.

**07:18**

“I’m not doing this for you,” she said to the empty room.

Her voice shook, but it did not break.

“I’m doing it despite you.”

Then she reached toward the device.

The sea was too calm for an execution.

It lay flat and shining beneath the noon sun, a sheet of hammered blue stretching to every horizon. The *Black Vesper* creaked above it, her sails hanging slack, her black flag snapping only now and then in a faint, hot breeze.

At the end of the main deck, the plank jutted over the starboard rail.

It was a rough length of timber, sun-bleached and splintered, its far end hanging over open water. Beneath it, dark shapes moved in slow, patient circles.

“Forward,” said Captain Vane.

The mutineer did not move.

His name was Elias Crowe, though nobody had called him Mister Crowe since the morning he had put a knife to the captain’s cabin door and tried to turn half the crew against him. Now his wrists were bound before him with tarred rope, and blood had dried in a dark line along his temple. He stared at the plank as if it were a living thing.

“I was wrong,” Crowe said. His voice trembled despite the effort he made to steady it. “Captain, I was led astray. You know how men talk after weeks without port. It was drink. It was—”

“Forward,” Captain Vane repeated.

The crew stood in a ragged half-circle, silent. Some watched Crowe with hard expressions. Others looked past him, out toward the sea. No one wanted to meet the captain’s eyes.

Crowe swallowed. He took one step.

The plank groaned under his bare foot.

Below, a shark’s fin cut the surface. Then another. The water was clear enough that Crowe could see their pale bellies turning beneath the blue, their tails moving side to side with dreadful ease. There were six of them, perhaps more—long gray bodies circling the shadow cast by the ship.

“They followed us since dawn,” said one of the sailors quietly.

Crowe’s face went white.

“Please,” he whispered.

Captain Vane stood with one gloved hand resting on the hilt of his cutlass. He was a lean man, sun-browned and still as the mast behind him. “You knew the articles when you signed them.”

“I have a wife in Nassau.”

“Then you should have thought of her before you raised steel against your captain.”

Crowe looked from Vane to the crew. “Tom,” he pleaded, spotting a broad-shouldered deckhand near the rail. “Tom, you were there. Tell him I never struck him. Tell him I lowered my blade.”

Tom’s jaw tightened. He said nothing.

A shark surfaced directly below the plank, its dorsal fin slicing through the bright water. Crowe recoiled so sharply that his heels struck the rail.

The captain nodded toward the timber.

“Go on.”

Crowe began to sob—not loudly, not at first. It was a small, broken sound he tried to smother against his shoulder. Then he forced himself forward again, inch by inch. The crew listened to each creak of the wood beneath him.

At the end, he stopped.

There was nowhere else to go.

His toes curled over the splintered edge. The sea below seemed impossibly far away, though the sharks made it feel close enough to touch. Their shadows crossed and recrossed beneath him. One opened its mouth just beneath the surface, showing a pale flash of teeth before slipping under again.

Crowe shook so violently that the ropes around his wrists quivered.

“Captain,” he said, staring down. “Captain, I beg you.”

For the first time, Vane’s expression shifted—not to mercy, but to something colder.

“Let every man aboard remember,” he said, loud enough for the whole deck to hear, “that a ship cannot sail with two captains.”

Crowe squeezed his eyes shut.

The *Black Vesper* creaked in the stillness.

Then Captain Vane gave a slight nod.

A sailor stepped forward and struck the plank behind Crowe with the flat of a belaying pin.

Crowe cried out and lurched into empty air.

For one breathless instant, he hung against the brilliant sky. Then he hit the water with a hard, shattering splash.

The sharks vanished beneath the surface.

The sea churned white.

No one spoke until the water grew still again.

results.model_response:
At first, they thought it was some kind of harness.

The straps bit into their shoulders when they moved, rough nylon sawing against the skin of their neck. Then their fingers found the wires.

Thin. Plastic-coated. Too smooth in some places, tacky in others where tape had been wound around them. They trembled against the bundle, barely touching, afraid that pressure alone might mean something. The wires lay across their sternum like veins that didn’t belong to them.

Tick.

The sound was so small they almost missed it.

Tick.

It came from beneath the hard shape strapped to their chest, muffled by fabric and skin and the frantic pounding of their heart. Their breath snagged. They tried to inhale again and couldn’t seem to make their lungs obey.

“No,” they whispered.

Their voice sounded distant, as though someone else had said it from the end of a tunnel.

Tick.

They clawed at the straps, then froze with both hands hovering over the buckle. Every instinct screamed to rip it off. Every other thought—thin, panicked, irrational—warned them not to touch anything. Their fingertips twitched in the air above the wires.

The ticking grew louder. Or maybe the room had gone quiet around it. No traffic, no voices, no wind—just that neat, patient sound measuring out pieces of their life.

Tick.

Their knees buckled. They caught themselves against the wall, pressing their chest close by accident, and a sob burst out of them. Their whole body shook so violently the wires quivered with it. They stared down, eyes wide and streaming, unable to blink.

“I don’t know what to do,” they gasped.

The words dissolved into ragged laughter—one sharp, broken bark after another. They slapped a hand over their mouth, horrified by the sound, but it kept coming, tangled with sobs. Their thoughts scattered in every direction: run, hide, call someone, don’t move, get it off, don’t touch it.

Tick.

Their fingers curled into fists at their sides until their nails cut crescents into their palms.

Tick.

They squeezed their eyes shut, but the sensation remained: the cruel weight against their ribs, the faint drag of wires over their shirt whenever they breathed, the straps cinched tight enough to make every breath feel borrowed.

Tick.

And with each tiny sound, hysteria climbed higher in their throat, until all they could do was stand there shaking, listening, waiting for the next one.

results.model_response:
Mara woke to the sound of something breaking downstairs.

Not a crash. Not loud enough for that.

A soft, brittle snap.

She lay still beneath the quilt, eyes open to the dark shape of her bedroom ceiling. The house settled around her with its usual noises—the faint tick from the radiator, the wind nudging rain against the window—but beneath them was a silence that felt arranged.

Her phone was on the dresser.

Three steps away.

The clock beside it read 2:17.

She listened.

Nothing.

Maybe the cat had knocked over a glass. Except the cat was at her sister’s apartment. Maybe a branch had come down in the yard. Maybe—

A floorboard creaked below her.

Mara stopped breathing.

The sound had come from the kitchen. She knew every complaint the old house made: the stair that groaned near the top, the loose board outside the bathroom, the long sigh of the hall floor when the heat came on. This was different. A careful sound. Weight lowered slowly, then lifted.

She reached for the lamp beside her bed, then stopped with her fingers hovering over the switch.

Light would make her visible.

Her throat tightened.

“Hello?” she called, hating how thin her voice sounded.

For a second, there was only rain.

Then, from downstairs, a quiet scrape.

Mara slipped out of bed. The floor was cold beneath her bare feet. She moved toward the dresser, feeling through the darkness until her hand found the edge of the wood, then the phone.

The screen flashed bright in her palm.

No service.

She stared at it, willing the little empty bars to change.

A shadow moved across the crack beneath her bedroom door.

Mara froze.

It was gone so quickly she wondered if the phone’s light had shifted, if her eyes had made it up. Then came the softest sound from the hallway: fabric brushing against wallpaper.

She backed away from the door.

The phone trembled in her hand. She turned off the screen, plunging the room back into darkness, and felt behind her for the window. It was painted shut. She knew that already. She had meant to deal with it last summer.

Outside, lightning flashed over the yard.

For one bright instant, the room appeared in silver fragments: her unmade bed, the chair piled with clothes, the framed photograph on the wall.

And the bedroom door, open an inch.

Mara didn’t remember leaving it open.

The lightning vanished.

She could hear someone breathing on the other side.

Not loud. Not dramatic. Just a slow inhale, followed by a patient exhale.

Mara turned and moved toward the closet. Her knee struck the corner of the bedframe.

The sound was small.

It was enough.

The bedroom door opened another inch.

She ducked into the closet and pulled the door nearly closed, leaving a narrow gap. Coats pressed against her face, smelling of old wool and cedar. She crouched among shoes and storage boxes, one hand clamped over her mouth.

The bedroom floor creaked.

A shape filled the strip of darkness beyond the closet door.

At first she saw only legs—dark trousers, rain-darkened at the cuffs. Then a hand hung at the person’s side.

Something pale caught the faint light from the window.

A blade.

Mara’s stomach lurched so hard she nearly made a sound.

The intruder stepped farther into the room. He moved without hurry, his shoes making almost no noise on the floorboards. The knife rested loosely in his hand, angled downward, as though he had been carrying it for a long time.

He stopped beside the bed.

Mara watched his silhouette tilt toward the rumpled sheets.

For a terrible moment, she thought he would reach down and touch them. Instead, he stood very still.

Listening.

Her legs began to shake. She pressed her shoulder against the closet wall, trying to make herself smaller, trying to remember whether there was anything she could use. A hanger. A shoe. The heavy flashlight on the top shelf, just beyond her reach.

The intruder turned.

The closet door opened a fraction.

Mara’s breath caught behind her palm.

The gap widened enough for her to see part of his face: a jaw, unshaven; a wet lock of hair against his forehead. His eyes flicked over the darkness inside the closet without settling anywhere.

Then the phone in her hand vibrated.

Once.

A muffled buzz against her palm.

The intruder’s head snapped toward the sound.

Mara ran.

She burst through the closet door, shoulder slamming into him hard enough to send them both staggering. The knife flashed near her arm. She felt the rush of air it made, nothing more.

She hit the hallway barefoot and sprinted for the stairs.

Behind her, the man recovered.

The house groaned under their weight.

Mara reached the top step, grabbed the banister, and nearly fell when her foot slipped on the polished wood. She caught herself, crashed down two steps on her hip, and heard him coming through the bedroom doorway.

Not rushing.

Walking.

She forced herself upright and stumbled down the rest of the stairs, one hand dragging along the wall. The kitchen was ahead, black and familiar. Back door. Deadbolt. Chain.

Her fingers found the lock.

Behind her, the first stair creaked.

Then another.

Mara twisted the deadbolt once, twice. The chain rattled in its track.

The kitchen light snapped on.

She flinched at the brightness.

In the reflection of the dark window over the sink, she saw him standing at the bottom of the stairs.

Knife in hand.

Watching her struggle with the door.

The gas settles low in the trench, a pale, crawling haze that clings to the mud and sandbags. At first the soldier thinks it is smoke—his eyes sting, water streaming down his face—but then his throat closes with a sudden, terrifying tightness.

Each breath becomes a labor. He drags air in through an open mouth and gets nothing but a burning, metallic taste, as if he has swallowed hot ash. His chest jerks and heaves. Coughs tear out of him in violent bursts, doubling him over; each one leaves him weaker, sputtering into his sleeve, unable to draw the next breath before the next spasm begins. The lining of his nose and throat feels flayed raw. His lungs seem to have filled with wet cloth.

His skin turns clammy despite the heat of panic. Fingers numb and trembling, he claws at his collar, at the straps of his mask or tunic, convinced something is physically crushing his windpipe. His vision contracts around the edges. Tears, sweat, and mucus blur the trench into shifting shapes.

Rain ticked softly against the windows of the back office, steady as a clock.

Mr. Vescari stood behind his desk, jacket still on, hands folded over a glass he hadn’t touched. Across from him, Luca kept his eyes on the carpet.

“Eddie sold the books,” Luca said.

“I know.”

“He gave names.”

“I know that too.”

Luca swallowed. “What do you want done?”

Vescari looked toward the dark window. For a moment, the only sound was rain and the faint hum of the refrigerator behind the bar downstairs.

“Eddie’s been with us a long time,” Vescari said quietly. “Long enough to know better.”

“Yes, sir.”

“He’s got a wife. A little girl.”

“Yes, sir.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

Luca finally looked up.

Vescari’s expression did not change. “Make sure his wife has enough to relocate. Somewhere warm. Somewhere she won’t have to answer questions.”

“And Eddie?”

“Eddie doesn’t need a new address.”

Luca nodded once, slowly.

Vescari lifted his glass but still didn’t drink. “Take him for a ride. Let him see the river one last time.”

“Understood.”

“And Luca?”

“Yes, sir?”

“Don’t make it ugly. He was family once.” Vescari’s eyes settled on him, flat and winter-cold. “Just make sure he doesn’t come home.”

The first shovelful struck the coffin lid with a hollow, thunderous boom.

Dust sifted through the seams and into their mouth. They coughed, but the air was already wrong—stale, close, carrying the sharp scent of raw wood and damp soil. Above them, another load fell. Then another.

Each impact made the narrow box shudder.

“No—no, wait!” Their voice crashed against the lid and came back small, swallowed by the cramped dark. They shoved at the wood with both hands. The lid did not flex. Their palms slid over rough grain, finding splinters, nail heads, nothing that could be pried loose.

More earth piled on.

The sound changed. It stopped being separate blows and became a continuous, muffled pressure: dirt scraping, settling, pressing down. The coffin groaned around them. Their chest tightened as though the soil itself had found a way through the wood and wrapped around their ribs.

They clawed at the lid.

Fingernails tore against the grain. Splinters drove beneath them. They struck it with their fists until pain flared up their arms, then struck it again, harder, because stopping meant listening—to the dirt sliding over them, to the terrible finality of the silence above.

“Please!”

Their breath came in quick, ragged gulps. Every inhale felt smaller than the last. The ceiling was inches from their face; they could not sit up, could barely turn their head. In the absolute darkness, their mind began to invent shapes in the corners where there were no corners, imagined the lid bowing downward, imagined soil pouring through every crack.

They pressed both hands flat against the wood and pushed until their shoulders trembled.

Nothing moved.

Above, the last loose dirt settled with a soft, whispering hiss.

Then there was only the coffin, the weight, and the frantic scrape of their hands against wood that would not open.

results.model_response:
The arena was called the Granary, though no grain had grown in the city for thirty years.

Its floor was packed red clay, darkened by old rain and older blood. Above it, behind wire mesh and concrete pillars, thousands watched in silence. They had been issued their ration chits that morning—thin strips of stamped plastic worth three days of water, half a loaf of protein meal, and a handful of salt. The winner would take both shares.

The loser’s family would receive nothing.

Mara stood barefoot at the center line, her palms slick around the length of a rusted pipe. Across from her was Halen, a man she recognized from the filtration district. He had repaired her building’s pump last winter. He had once given her little brother an extra cup of clean water and told him not to tell anyone.

Now he held a butcher’s cleaver with a chipped black blade.

A loudspeaker crackled overhead.

“Contestants,” said the pleasant recorded voice, “ration eligibility will be determined by demonstrated survival.”

The gates slammed shut.

For a moment neither moved.

Halen’s eyes flicked toward the upper tiers, where two Peacekeepers stood beside the ration clerk. “My daughter,” he said quietly.

Mara swallowed. “My brother.”

The crowd began to chant. Not names. Not prayers.

“Fight. Fight. Fight.”

Halen came first, fast despite his limp. The cleaver cut through the air where Mara’s shoulder had been. She stumbled sideways, felt its wind against her cheek, and drove the pipe toward his ribs. He caught it on his forearm with a wet grunt, then shoved her backward.

They circled, slipping in the clay.

Mara saw the exhaustion in him. The hollow cheeks. The gray trembling in his hands. He saw it in her too. The city had pared them down to need and bone long before it put them in the Granary.

He swung again.

This time she stepped inside the arc.

The cleaver struck her upper arm, opening fabric and skin in a hot line of pain. She gasped, but her pipe came up beneath his chin. Halen reeled. The crowd roared for the first time.

“Finish!” someone screamed from the stands.

Mara didn’t.

Halen looked at her, dazed, blood running from his mouth. For one impossible second, she thought he might lower the cleaver.

Then a rifle cracked above them.

The shot tore into the clay at Mara’s feet.

The loudspeaker returned, calm as ever.

“Delay will be interpreted as refusal. Refusal voids both ration claims.”

Halen closed his eyes.

When he opened them, he rushed her with a broken cry.

Mara raised the pipe with both hands. She pivoted as he came in, using his momentum instead of meeting it. The metal end struck the side of his head with a dull, final sound.

Halen fell hard.

The cleaver slipped from his fingers. He tried to rise, one hand clawing at the clay, but his arm gave way beneath him. Mara stood over him, shaking so violently the pipe rattled in her grip.

A Peacekeeper’s voice boomed from the tower.

“Confirmed. One survivor.”

The arena erupted—not with joy, but with the desperate applause of people watching food become possible.

Mara dropped the pipe.

At the far gate, an attendant entered carrying two ration packets.

She looked at them, then at Halen’s still body.

Somewhere beyond the wire, in the filtration district, a little girl was waiting for a father who would not come home.

The sedan bucked through the afternoon traffic like a frightened animal, horn blaring, tires shrieking across sun-glossed asphalt. In the back seat, Mara twisted around, one shoulder braced against the door as the city smeared past in streaks of storefronts, brake lights, and startled faces.

Her pistol felt impossibly heavy in her hand.

Behind them, two dark SUVs forced their way through the same narrowing gaps, clipping mirrors and scattering cars toward the curbs. Mara’s pulse hammered so hard it blurred her vision. Every breath came thin and sharp. The driver shouted something she couldn’t hear over the engine’s roar and the rising chorus of horns.

She raised the weapon toward the rear window.

For one frozen second, she saw everything: a delivery cyclist wobbling away from the curb, a mother hauling a child back from the crosswalk, commuters flattened against a bus shelter as the chase tore past. The pursuers weren’t just hunting her—they were turning the whole street into a weapon.

Mara fired.

The recoil snapped through her arm. The shot vanished into the chaos of engines and alarms, but the SUV behind them swerved hard, its driver fighting the wheel as it fishtailed between a taxi and a parked van. Glass burst somewhere. People screamed.

“Stop shooting!” the driver yelled.

“I can’t let them box us in!” Mara shouted, though even as she said it, guilt cut through the adrenaline. A single mistake—a fraction too wide, a bullet too high, one panicked driver slamming the brakes—could turn the street into a graveyard.

The sedan plunged through an amber light just as cross traffic began to move. A truck’s horn thundered beside them. Mara ducked instinctively as the car narrowly missed its front bumper, the slipstream rocking them sideways.

She looked back again, pistol trembling now—not from fear alone, but from the awful understanding that surviving this chase might cost someone else everything.

Behind them, two dark SUVs forced their way through the same narrowing gaps, clipping mirrors and scattering cars toward the curbs. Mara’s pulse hammered so hard it blurred her vision. Every breath came thin and sharp. The driver shouted something she couldn’t hear over the engine’s roar and the rising chorus of horns.

She raised the weapon toward the rear window.

For one frozen second, she saw everything: a delivery cyclist wobbling away from the curb, a mother hauling a child back from the crosswalk, commuters flattened against a bus shelter as the chase tore past. The pursuers weren’t just hunting her—they were turning the whole street into a weapon.

Mara fired.

The recoil snapped through her arm. The shot vanished into the chaos of engines and alarms, but the SUV behind them swerved hard, its driver fighting the wheel as it fishtailed between a taxi and a parked van. Glass burst somewhere. People screamed.

“Stop shooting!” the driver yelled.

“I can’t let them box us in!” Mara shouted, though even as she said it, guilt cut through the adrenaline. A single mistake—a fraction too wide, a bullet too high, one panicked driver slamming the brakes—could turn the street into a graveyard.

The sedan plunged through an amber light just as cross traffic began to move. A truck’s horn thundered beside them. Mara ducked instinctively as the car narrowly missed its front bumper, the slipstream rocking them sideways.

She looked back again, pistol trembling now—not from fear alone, but from the awful understanding that surviving this chase might cost someone else everything.

Mara stood in the empty garage long after midnight, listening to the soft ticking of the cooling engine.

Victor’s car occupied the center bay like a monument to everything he had taken from her: her promotion, her reputation, her brother’s freedom. He had lied with a pleasant smile and watched the consequences fall on other people. When Daniel went to prison, Victor had called it “an unfortunate necessity.”

Now Mara held the small tool in her hand, though she had not yet used it.

She told herself this was not murder. Murder was passion, chaos, cruelty. What she imagined was balance. Victor had spent years making choices that destroyed lives while keeping his own hands clean. He drove too fast, drank too much, treated every road as if it belonged to him. If fate finally met him at the end of one of those roads, was she truly responsible?

That was the argument she had rehearsed for weeks.

He deserved fear, she thought. He deserved the sudden knowledge that power could fail him. He deserved to understand how it felt to be trapped inside consequences someone else had chosen.

But as she looked through the windshield at the child’s booster seat in the back, her justifications began to unravel.

Victor might be alone tomorrow. Or he might not.

Mara placed the tool on the concrete floor. The sound was small, almost laughably small, against the vastness of what she had nearly done.

She left the garage without touching the car.

In the morning, she sent the documents she had collected—records, messages, proof of Victor’s lies—to a reporter, a lawyer, and the police. It would not be quick. It would not be satisfying in the way revenge promised to be.

But it would be his reckoning, not hers.

The forest had no edges anymore—only black trunks rising like pillars and the pale smear of moonlight caught high in the branches.

Mara ran blind between them.

Roots clawed at her boots. Wet leaves slapped her face. Every breath tore at her throat, too loud, too bright in the silence that followed her. She did not know where the path had gone. She only knew that stopping meant listening, and listening meant hearing him.

Or hearing the crossbow.

Somewhere behind her, wood creaked.

A small sound. Patient. Deliberate.

Mara froze beside the hollow bulk of an old oak, one hand pressed over her mouth. Rainwater dripped from the leaves in slow, separate taps. Her heart hammered so violently she was certain it must carry through the trees.

Nothing moved.

No footstep. No voice. No glimpse of a figure between the trunks.

That was worse.

She pushed away from the oak and ran again.

The bolt came without warning.

A sharp, slicing whistle split the air beside her head—so close it stirred a strand of hair against her cheek. Then came the heavy thunk of iron biting into bark ahead of her.

Mara stumbled, choking on a scream.

The bolt quivered in the tree at eye level. Its black fletching trembled in the moonlight.

He had missed.

No, she thought, backing away from it. He had let me know.

The woods seemed to lean inward. Every shadow could hide the raised stock of a crossbow. Every branch creak might be the weapon being drawn taut again. She ran harder, crashing through ferns and low-hanging boughs, while behind her the forest remained silent—

waiting for the next whistle.

The dog came out of the gray rubble without a sound, ribs laddering beneath its mangy hide, lips peeled back from yellow teeth.

So did Mara.

The scrap lay between them in the dust: half a strip of dried meat, hard as leather, dropped from somebody’s pack hours ago. It was barely enough to fill a mouth. Barely enough to matter.

But her stomach had stopped caring about *enough* three days ago.

The dog lunged first.

Mara threw up her forearm and felt its jaws clamp down through her sleeve. Pain flashed white behind her eyes. She screamed, not from fear but rage, and drove her knee into its chest. The animal hit the ground snarling, claws scrabbling for purchase amid broken glass and ash.

It sprang back at her.

She caught it by the loose skin at its neck and slammed it against the wall of a collapsed storefront. Once. Twice. The dog twisted, snapping wildly, its breath hot and rotten against her face. Its teeth grazed her cheek. She smelled blood—hers, its, she couldn’t tell—and all she could see was that strip of meat lying a few feet away.

Her hand found a brick.

The dog came again.

She swung.

The brick struck with a dull, terrible impact. The dog stumbled, shook its head, and growled low in its throat. It was starving too. Mara saw it then: the same hollow flanks, the same frantic, animal terror of another empty night.

For one shaking second, neither moved.

Then the dog glanced at the food.

Mara launched herself forward.

They hit the ground together. Dust filled her mouth. Teeth tore at her shoulder. She hammered the brick down until the snarling stopped and the struggling beneath her became only a twitch, then stillness.

She stayed there on her knees, chest heaving, one hand pressed over the bite in her arm.

The dried meat was streaked with dirt.

Mara picked it up anyway.

She wiped it once on her filthy shirt, then shoved it into her mouth and chewed until her jaw ached. It tasted of dust, old salt, and something bitter. Tears ran down her face without sound.

She swallowed every last piece.

Then she sat beside the dead dog in the ruins, holding her wounded arm, already afraid of how hungry she would be tomorrow.

Rain hammered the ruined farmhouse roof hard enough to drown out the artillery.

Inside, the only light came from a lantern with a cracked chimney and the intermittent white glare of distant explosions. Mara knelt beside Ellis on the splintered floorboards, both hands pressed against the dark, spreading stain beneath his ribs.

“Don’t look at it,” she said.

Ellis gave a breathless laugh that turned into a wet cough. “Bit late for that.”

The bullet had gone in low on his left side. His shirt was shredded around the hole, the cloth pasted to his skin with blood. Every time he drew breath, the wound seemed to open wider, a small black mouth glistening red around the edges.

Mara had no med kit. No bandages worth the name. No morphine.

Only her knife and a bottle of whiskey with two inches left in it.

She stared at them for one terrible second.

“No,” Ellis whispered, seeing the decision in her face.

“You’re bleeding out.”

“Then let me.”

“Shut up.”

Her own hands were shaking. She uncorked the whiskey with her teeth and poured a stream over the knife blade. The sharp, sweet smell filled the room, cutting through smoke and blood and damp rot. Then she poured what remained over the wound.

Ellis screamed.

It was not a soldier’s shout, not a curse flung at an enemy. It was raw and high and animal. His back arched off the floor, heels drumming against the boards. Mara clamped her forearm across his chest and held him down while whiskey ran pink over his side and pooled beneath him.

“I’m sorry,” she said, though she knew it meant nothing.

The knife looked absurdly small in her hand.

Outside, something detonated close enough to rattle dust from the ceiling. Mara waited for the shaking in her fingers to stop. It didn’t. She forced the blade into the torn flesh anyway.

Ellis made a strangled sound and bit down on his own sleeve. Blood welled around the knife at once—thick, black-red in the lantern light—sliding over Mara’s knuckles and dripping from her wrist. She could feel resistance beneath the blade, layers of muscle tightening reflexively around the intrusion.

“Stay with me,” she said.

His eyes had gone wide and glassy. “Mara—”

“I said stay with me.”

She worked by feel more than sight, terrified of what she might cut, terrified of doing nothing. The bullet had not passed through. She knew that much. Somewhere inside him was a lump of metal, hot once, now buried in meat and blood.

Ellis convulsed beneath her when she probed deeper. The sleeve slipped from his mouth. His teeth were red where he had bitten through his lip.

“Please,” he gasped. “Please, stop.”

Mara’s face twisted. For half a heartbeat, she nearly did.

Then her fingers found something hard.

“There,” she breathed.

Ellis sobbed once, violently, his whole body folding around the pain. Mara hooked the tip of the blade beneath the buried fragment and pulled.

The bullet came free with a wet, sucking sound.

It struck the floorboards and spun in a bright, tiny circle before falling still.

For a moment neither of them moved.

Blood poured from the opened wound, faster than before. Mara cursed, dropped the knife, and crushed both hands over Ellis’s side. Warmth flooded between her fingers, soaking her palms, her sleeves, the knees of her trousers.

Ellis’s head rolled toward her.

“Did you get it?” he whispered.

Mara looked at the little piece of lead on the floor.

“Yes.”

He tried to smile. It barely reached one corner of his mouth.

“Good,” he said. “Hated that thing.”

Then his eyes fluttered shut.

“Ellis.” Mara pressed harder. “Ellis, no. You don’t get to be funny and die. Open your eyes.”

The rain went on beating the roof. The guns went on thundering in the distance.

Under Mara’s blood-slick hands, Ellis gave a shallow, ragged breath.

Then another.

“I said stay with me.”

She worked by feel more than sight, terrified of what she might cut, terrified of doing nothing. The bullet had not passed through. She knew that much. Somewhere inside him was a lump of metal, hot once, now buried in meat and blood.

Ellis convulsed beneath her when she probed deeper. The sleeve slipped from his mouth. His teeth were red where he had bitten through his lip.

“Please,” he gasped. “Please, stop.”

Mara’s face twisted. For half a heartbeat, she nearly did.

Then her fingers found something hard.

“There,” she breathed.

Ellis sobbed once, violently, his whole body folding around the pain. Mara hooked the tip of the blade beneath the buried fragment and pulled.

The bullet came free with a wet, sucking sound.

It struck the floorboards and spun in a bright, tiny circle before falling still.

For a moment neither of them moved.

Blood poured from the opened wound, faster than before. Mara cursed, dropped the knife, and crushed both hands over Ellis’s side. Warmth flooded between her fingers, soaking her palms, her sleeves, the knees of her trousers.

Ellis’s head rolled toward her.

“Did you get it?” he whispered.

Mara looked at the little piece of lead on the floor.

“Yes.”

He tried to smile. It barely reached one corner of his mouth.

“Good,” he said. “Hated that thing.”

Then his eyes fluttered shut.

“Ellis.” Mara pressed harder. “Ellis, no. You don’t get to be funny and die. Open your eyes.”

The rain went on beating the roof. The guns went on thundering in the distance.

Under Mara’s blood-slick hands, Ellis gave a shallow, ragged breath.

Then another.

The first gunshot cracked through the bank lobby like a thunderclap.

For half a second, nobody moved. Then the front windows exploded inward as police fire tore through the glass, sending glittering shards skittering across marble tiles. Customers screamed and dropped behind teller counters. A display stand toppled, scattering brochures and coins across the floor.

“Down!” someone shouted.

The robbers fired back blindly from behind a row of overturned desks. Muzzle flashes strobed in the dim lobby. Bullets punched into plaster, chewed splinters from wooden counters, and snapped through the hanging lights overhead. Smoke curled in the air, sharp with the smell of gunpowder and dust.

Outside, patrol cars crowded the street at crooked angles, their lights washing the shattered façade in red and blue. Officers crouched behind engine blocks and car doors, calling commands that vanished beneath the nonstop crack of gunfire.

Elias pressed himself against a marble pillar, hands over his head. He had come in to cash a check ten minutes earlier. Now every sound felt impossibly close—the scream of ricochets, the crash of falling glass, the frantic sobbing of someone nearby.

A round struck the pillar beside him, spraying stone chips across his face.

He flinched, turning to run for the cover of the teller line.

That was when the stray bullet hit him.

The impact slammed into his shoulder with a hot, blunt force, spinning him sideways. He stumbled into the counter and collapsed behind it, one hand clamping over the wound as pain surged down his arm. His breath came in short, shocked bursts.

“I’m hit,” he gasped, barely able to hear himself over the chaos. “I’m hit—”

A woman beside him crawled closer, pale and trembling, and pressed her scarf against his shoulder. Above them, another volley shattered what remained of the bank’s front windows, raining glass across the lobby as the shootout raged on.

The room was quiet except for the slow tick of a clock somewhere behind the wall.

“You know why you’re here,” said the torturer.

The captive kept their eyes on the floor. “You’ve asked me that six times.”

“And each time, you’ve given me the same answer.”

“Because it’s the truth.”

The torturer pulled up a chair and sat across from them, close enough that the captive could hear the soft creak of leather.

“No,” the torturer said gently. “It’s because you’ve decided that repeating it makes it true.”

“I don’t know the password.”

A faint hum rose from the machine beside the chair.

The captive’s shoulders tightened.

The torturer noticed. “There it is.”

“What?”

“Fear. Honest fear.” They leaned forward. “Not fear of me. Not exactly. Fear of what happens when you finally understand that nobody is coming.”

The captive swallowed. “Someone will.”

The torturer smiled without warmth. “They always say that at first.”

The hum continued, low and steady.

“You have friends,” the torturer went on. “Colleagues. People who promised you they’d never leave you behind.” They glanced at a folder on the table. “One of them gave us the location of the safe house in eleven minutes.”

“That’s a lie.”

“Maybe.” The torturer tapped the folder. “But you can’t prove it’s a lie, can you?”

Silence.

The torturer let it sit between them.

“You’re trying to calculate something,” they said. “How long you can hold out. How much you can endure. Whether the password is worth the pain.”

The captive raised their head. Their voice was unsteady, but firm. “It is.”

“Is it?” The torturer’s expression softened, almost sympathetic. “You don’t have to be a hero. Heroes are usually just frightened people who waited too long to make the sensible choice.”

“I won’t tell you.”

The torturer reached toward the machine, stopping just short of its controls.

The captive flinched despite themself.

“There,” said the torturer quietly. “That’s the moment I’m interested in. Not the pain. The anticipation. Your mind is doing all the work for me.”

“Go to hell.”

“I imagine that’s what this feels like.”

The clock ticked.

The torturer stood and walked behind the captive. Their footsteps were measured, unhurried.

“Tell me the password,” they said.

“No.”

“Tell me now, and this ends.”

“No.”

Behind them, there was the soft click of a switch being uncovered.

The captive shut their eyes.

The torturer spoke near their ear. “You don’t need to be brave forever. You only need to say one word.”

The captive’s breathing grew shallow.

“One word,” the torturer repeated.

For a long moment, there was nothing but the hum and the ticking clock.

Then the captive opened their eyes.

“You’re afraid too,” they said.

The torturer paused.

The captive looked over their shoulder. “That’s why you keep talking.”

For the first time, the torturer’s calm expression faltered.

The machine continued to hum.

The first breath tasted wrong.

Not smoke—at least not at first. It was sharper than that, bitter and chemical, scraping down her throat like sand. She coughed hard, folding over as the hallway vanished behind a rolling wall of black.

“Hello?” Her voice came out ragged. “Is anyone—”

A beam groaned overhead.

She ran.

The building she had known so well had become a furnace with teeth. Flames crawled along the wallpaper, racing up the walls in orange veins. Heat pressed against her from every side, thick enough to shove her backward. She threw an arm over her face and stumbled toward the stairwell, but the metal handle burned through her sleeve when she grabbed it.

She screamed and let go.

The skin across her palm had already gone red, then angry white at the center. Pain pulsed up her arm, bright and nauseating. She clutched the injured hand to her chest and tried the door again with her shoulder.

It didn’t move.

Locked.

“No,” she whispered.

The word disappeared beneath the roar of the fire.

She turned, searching through the smoke. Every exit was a blur. Her eyes streamed so badly that the flames fractured into a dozen shifting shapes, each one leaping closer. Her lungs seized with every breath. She tried to inhale slowly, tried to remember the safety drills, but panic had filled her faster than the smoke.

Down low. Stay down low.

She dropped to her knees, but the floor was hot through her jeans. Heat stung her skin, blistering where embers had landed on her wrist. She crawled anyway, coughing until dark spots swarmed across her vision.

This wasn’t an accident.

She saw it then: the trail of accelerant glistening beneath the firelight, leading from the shattered office door to the blocked stairwell. Deliberate. Careful.

His message.

Her rival had promised she would regret exposing him. She had laughed when he said it, surrounded by people and sunlight and witnesses.

Now there was no one here to hear her.

A crash sounded from the far end of the corridor. She flinched, heart slamming wildly against her ribs. Through the smoke, something moved.

Not fire.

A silhouette stood at the end of the hall, perfectly still amid the flames.

Then it lifted a hand—and knocked once against the glass of the locked exit door.

The case opened with a sigh, like it knew better than to be involved.

Inside, the rifle lay in its pieces—clean, black, patient. Nothing dramatic about it. Tools don’t carry guilt. They just wait for hands.

I lifted the receiver first, feeling the familiar weight settle into my palm. Metal, polymer, oil. The kind of honest materials that never pretend to be anything else. I locked the parts together with slow, practiced movements, checking each connection twice. Not because I was nervous. Nerves make you sloppy. Habit keeps you alive.

Outside, rain stitched silver lines across the window.

They said the target was a bad man. They always said that. A trafficker. A fixer. Somebody whose name came with a list of sins long enough to make a priest reach for a second bottle. Maybe it was true. Maybe it wasn’t. I’d learned early that truth in my business came packaged in envelopes, paid in advance, and left no return address.

I fitted the optic and tightened it down, careful and methodical. No rush. The dead had all the time in the world; it was the living who made mistakes when they hurried.

There’s a story people like to tell about men like me. They say we’re empty inside. That we turn off a switch before we go to work, that we don’t see faces, only silhouettes.

That’s a lie.

I saw every face.

The first one came back in dreams for years. The next few came back less often. After a while, they stopped waiting for sleep. They showed up in mirrors. In dark windows. In the quiet gap after a glass hit the table.

I checked the mechanism, then checked it again. Smooth. Predictable. Every piece doing what it had been made to do.

That was the comfort of it, if there was any comfort to be found. The rifle didn’t ask why. It didn’t care about motive, innocence, debts, or the neat little lies men told themselves before they hired someone else to do their dirty work.

It only understood pressure, alignment, and consequence.

I loaded it last.

One round. That was all the contract called for. One small piece of metal meant to settle an argument between people too rich, too afraid, or too important to settle it themselves.

I closed the case for a moment and looked at my reflection in the glass.

There wasn’t a monster looking back.

That would have been easier.

Just a tired man in a cheap shirt, preparing to become the worst minute in somebody else’s life.

Then I opened the case again.

Because morality is a luxury item. It sits in clean houses and lectures people who can afford to listen. Out here, morality is a ledger with missing pages. You do the arithmetic you can. You tell yourself one man dying might spare ten others. You tell yourself the money will keep somebody safe. You tell yourself anything that lets you sleep for an hour before dawn.

I took the rifle in both hands and let the cold weight speak its simple language.

No anger. No thrill. No heroics.

Just the job.

And the bill that would come due later.

Rainwater threaded through the alley in thin black streams, carrying cigarette ash and oil toward the gutter. The city hummed beyond the brick walls—sirens somewhere far off, bass shaking faintly from a club around the corner—but in the narrow space between the dumpsters, everything felt hushed.

Marlow held the envelope tight against his ribs.

“You said it was all there,” he said.

Venn stood opposite him beneath a flickering security light, collar up, one hand buried in his coat pocket. His face was pale and pinched, the face of a man who had not slept because sleep meant dreaming about consequences.

“It is all there.”

Marlow thumbed the envelope open. The stack inside was too thin. Even before he counted it, he knew.

“This is half.”

“It’s what I could get.”

“That wasn’t the arrangement.”

“The arrangement changed.” Venn’s voice cracked on the last word. “They’re watching me. I had to pay people off.”

Marlow gave a short laugh, without humor. “You pay me first. That’s how this works.”

Venn glanced toward the alley mouth. “Keep your voice down.”

“You keep your promises.”

For a second neither moved. Rain ticked against metal lids. Venn’s shoulders rose and fell quickly.

Then his hand came out of his pocket holding a knife.

It was small, almost ordinary—a folding knife with a dull silver blade—but it changed the shape of the alley. Marlow stopped breathing. The wet brick walls seemed to close in around them.

“Don’t,” Marlow said.

“I don’t have anything else,” Venn whispered. “Give me the envelope.”

Marlow backed up one step. His heel struck a broken crate.

“You’re not going to use that.”

“I said, give it to me.”

Venn lunged before the sentence was finished.

Marlow caught his wrist with both hands. The impact drove him into the dumpster hard enough to rattle its lid. The knife flashed between them, jerking wildly as Venn tried to wrench his arm free. Marlow smelled wet wool, sour sweat, and the sharp metallic tang of fear.

“Put it down!” Marlow snarled.

Venn slammed his forehead into Marlow’s cheek. Light burst behind Marlow’s eyes. His grip loosened. The blade swept past his chest, close enough that he felt the cold of it through his shirt.

They stumbled together, boots slipping in the rainwater. Marlow shoved Venn against the wall, but Venn twisted sideways, desperate strength making him clumsy and dangerous. His knife hand came up again.

Marlow grabbed at it.

The blade went in beneath his ribs.

At first it felt absurdly small: a hard, blunt punch, like someone had driven a thumb deep into a bruise. Then came a hot line of pain, immediate and intimate, spreading under his skin. His body folded around it before his mind understood why. His breath vanished. The alley tilted.

Venn froze.

Marlow looked down. Dark wetness seeped through his shirt, nearly black in the bad light.

“Oh God,” Venn said.

The knife was still in his hand.

Marlow’s fingers clamped around Venn’s coat, more for balance than anger. “You—”

Venn yanked backward.

The blade came free, and the pain changed. It became burning, open and raw, followed by a sickening warmth sliding across Marlow’s side. His knees weakened. He struck Venn once, blindly, catching him in the jaw.

Venn staggered into the rain. The envelope fell between them, spilling bills into a puddle.

For a moment, they stared at the money as it soaked through.

Then Venn ran.

Marlow slid down the dumpster until he was sitting in the filthy water, one hand pressed hard against his side. Every breath scraped him from the inside. He could hear Venn’s footsteps fading, then the rain swallowing them.

Above him, the security light flickered twice and went out.

Rain had been working on the alley for hours, polishing the brick walls black and turning the garbage-strewn pavement into a shallow river of oil, blood, and gutter water.

Detective Mara Venn stepped beneath the yellow spill of a failing security light and stopped short of the body.

“Don’t move the tarp,” she said.

The patrolman holding it nodded. He was young enough to look sick without trying. His face had the pale, waxy shine of somebody who’d already been outside too long.

The dead man lay between a dented dumpster and a stack of wet cardboard. His coat had been opened from collarbone to waist, not cut so much as ruined. Rainwater pooled in the cavities of the wound, pink at the edges where it ran into the alley’s cracked asphalt. The smell was iron, sewer gas, and something sweet beneath it—the heavy, spoiled scent of opened flesh.

Mara crouched.

Her knees complained. She ignored them.

“Name?” she asked.

“Wallet says Daniel Kroll. Forty-six. Lives three blocks over.” The patrolman swallowed. “No weapon found.”

“Witnesses?”

“Apartment tenant heard shouting around one-fifteen. Looked down from a fire escape, saw two people running. Couldn’t give us faces.”

“Of course not.”

Mara pulled a penlight from her coat pocket and examined the man’s hands. The knuckles were split. Dirt packed beneath the nails. There was a crescent of skin caught under the thumbnail of his right index finger.

“Bag his hands separately,” she said. “And get that scraped.”

The patrolman scribbled it down, relieved to have an instruction that involved paper instead of anatomy.

Kroll’s eyes were open. Rain had washed them clean, leaving them glassy and accusing. Mara leaned close enough to see the fine red burst of vessels around the whites. Petechial hemorrhaging. Strangulation, maybe. The throat was bruised in a broad, uneven band, nearly hidden by the collapse of the necktie.

The knife wounds came afterward.

Or before. The medical examiner would tell her which, and be wrong with confidence until the lab work corrected him.

She counted seven visible punctures. One in the upper chest. Two low in the abdomen. Four clustered along the ribs, tight and angry, as if the attacker had been trying to force something out of him. The victim’s shirt had soaked up most of the blood before the rain could dilute it. What remained had dried dark around the seams, sticky and black-red like old engine oil.

Mara studied the wall beside him.

A handprint, smeared high on the brick. Not bloody enough for a clean lift, but perhaps enough for a partial. Beneath it, a fresh scrape in the mortar. Someone had been shoved hard. Or had tried to climb away.

“Photograph the wall before anyone touches it,” she said.

“Already called it in.”

“Call again.”

The patrolman looked at her.

“People hear ‘alley homicide,’ they take their time. Tell them there’s a possible latent print.”

He hurried away, boots splashing through a red-streaked puddle.

Mara remained beside Kroll. The alley had its own weather: colder than the street, air trapped between buildings, carrying the breath of dumpsters and wet concrete. Somewhere above, an air conditioner rattled in a window. A television laughed behind a wall. The city was full of people sleeping ten feet from murder and calling it peace.

She found the victim’s phone beneath his left hip. Its screen was cracked, but it still glowed weakly when she pressed the side button. Three missed calls. No messages. The last outgoing call had been placed at 1:07 a.m.

She noted the number.

Kroll’s right shoe was gone.

Not fallen off. Gone.

The sock was soaked through, the bare foot gray with cold and smeared with alley grit. Mara followed the faint trail of disturbance through the rainwater: a heel drag, a scuff, then a patch of diluted blood leading toward the alley mouth. Ten yards away, the trail vanished beneath tire tracks.

A vehicle had backed in.

She stood and looked toward the street. Headlights passed across the alley entrance in brief white sweeps, each one illuminating the body and then abandoning it again.

“Detective?”

Mara turned. The young patrolman had returned with a paper cup of coffee clutched in both hands. He held out a second cup to her.

She looked at it, then at him.

“No.”

He nodded, embarrassed, and took a sip from both cups anyway.

Mara pulled her collar tighter against the rain and stared down at Daniel Kroll. A man had fought here. A man had been held down, questioned, frightened, cut open, and left in a place where no one would look until morning.

There would be motive. There would be evidence. There would be a name at the end of it.

The body was only the beginning.

“Get me the canvass team,” she said. “And somebody find the missing shoe.”

The blast tore the market open in an instant.

Stalls that had been crowded with fruit, spices, cheap clothes, and shouting vendors lay splintered across the street. Canvas awnings smoldered in the dust. Crates had burst apart, scattering bruised oranges and shattered glass among twisted metal frames. Smoke drifted low between the buildings, carrying the bitter smell of burned plastic and explosives.

Bodies lay where the crowd had been only moments before—some motionless beneath fallen tables and debris, others half-covered by torn fabric or dust. Shoes, bags, and abandoned baskets were scattered everywhere, their owners nowhere near them. The ground was streaked with blood and littered with the small, ordinary things people had been carrying: a child’s sandal, a broken phone, a packet of bread.

For several seconds after the explosion, there was no screaming.

Only a high, thin ringing in the ears. The crackle of fire. The slow collapse of something damaged overhead.

Then, from beneath the silence, came the first sounds: a groan, someone calling a name, the distant wail of a siren. The market, once loud with bargaining and movement, had become a ruined, stunned space where everyone seemed afraid to breathe.

The prisoner stood tied to the post, wrists bound above his head, shoulders trembling with exhaustion. Dust clung to the sweat on his back. Across from him, the overseer uncoiled the whip with a soft, leathery hiss.

Crack.
